entries.title: FMSNO: Scaling Surface Neural Operators by Learned Flow Matching Reparametrisation
entries.summary: We propose the Flow Matching Surface Neural Operator (FMSNO), which combines learning a shared map from irregular surface meshes to a regular two-dimensional grid on the sphere and training a neural operator on the regular grid. Constructing a separate map for each new geometry can dominate inference time on large meshes. We initially pretrain the mapping by flow matching using precomputed optimal transport maps as targets and then continue its training using combined geometry and CFD objectives. We apply it to unseen geometries in a single forward pass. The learned flow deforms the surface points, and we project its endpoints onto the sphere. We then splat geometric features onto the spherical grid, apply a neural operator (we tested both Fourier and Spherical Fourier Neural Operators), and interpolate its output back to the surface. For a mesh with $N$ points, evaluating the map costs O(N), and the full prediction costs O(NlogN) with the FNO backbone. We evaluate surface pressure prediction on ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, and drag coefficient prediction on DrivAerNet++. Across the three pressure benchmarks, our accuracy is on par with that of the most accurate baseline. On a surface with one million points, our method achieves a 354x end-to-end inference speedup over that baseline while keeping the same memory usage asymptotics of O(N).

entries.title: Support monotonicity for quadratically regularized optimal transport
entries.summary: We study the support of the optimizer $π_\varepsilon$ of the quadratically regularized optimal transport problem for quadratic cost and compactly supported marginals. As $\varepsilon$ tends to zero, this support converges to the support of the Monge coupling. We investigate whether the regularized supports are nested as $\varepsilon $ decreases. Under regularity assumptions on the marginal densities, their domains, and the Brenier map, we establish interior support inclusions in every dimension. More precisely, for each compact $K\subset\operatorname{int}X$ and fixed $θ\in(0,1)$, we prove that $\mathrm{spt}π_δ\cap(K\times Y) \subseteq\mathrm{spt}π_\varepsilon\cap(K\times Y)$ whenever $0<δ\leθ\varepsilon $ and $\varepsilon$ is sufficiently small. On these points, the rescaled density $\varepsilon dπ_\varepsilon/d(μ\otimesν)$ is bounded below by a positive multiple of $\varepsilon^{2/(d+2)}$. Our analysis combines sharp potential estimates with affine rescaling and a Liouville theorem that identifies the unique limiting density of the rescaled problem.

entries.title: Bismut formula and applications for conditional McKean-Vlasov SDEs driven by fractional Brownian motion
entries.summary: We investigate the stability of Lions derivatives under transition-rate perturbations for conditional McKean-Vlasov SDEs driven by fractional Brownian motion with $H>1/2$. For bounded measurable terminal functions, we establish Lions differentiability, a Bismut formula, and a gradient estimate under bounded first-order drift derivatives with suitable Hölder regularity, without imposing additional higher-order regularity assumptions on the drift's Lions derivative. Fractional Volterra estimates accommodate switching-induced discontinuities, while the Bismut weight has a common representation in terms of the switching process for all admissible transition-rate matrices. Combining this representation with likelihood-ratio methods, we prove quantitative stability, Fréchet differentiability, and a quadratic remainder estimate for Lions derivatives under perturbations preserving the positive off-diagonal support. In a nonlinear two-state model, the quadratic remainder estimate holds uniformly over terminal threshold events. We also demonstrate nonzero transition-rate sensitivity of Lions derivatives under fractional noise, whereas the corresponding Brownian model has a rate-independent terminal law.

entries.title: SF-Flow: Spectral Flow Matching with High Structural Fidelity for Hallucination-Suppressed Scientific Image Generation
entries.summary: Scientific image generation focuses on reproducing experimental appearance while following a prescribed spatial layout. A key challenge is acute data sparsity, which requires operating with unpaired collections of materials (real images and prescribed layouts), where no direct supervision is feasible. Work on unpaired translation has shown that it is possible to reproduce the texture and intensity variations of real images, but it is extremely hard to retain the intended phase boundaries in the prescribed locations. This paper tackles this challenge and introduces SF-Flow, a flow-matching model trained only on real material images that imposes spectral constraints during generation, producing images that are high-fidelity and consistent with the prescribed layouts. Because layouts enter only at generation time, the approach extends to layout maps outside the distribution of any available training layouts. We evaluate the method on synchrotron tomography of concrete, lens-coupled laboratory microCT of powders, and industrial XCT of additively manufactured metal. Without instrument-specific modeling, we show that SF-Flow achieves substantially higher template agreement and joint fidelity--structure score than previous methods, including contrastive unpaired translation.

entries.title: PsyDrift: Healthy-Reference Latent Diffusion for Anomaly Scoring in Autism Spectrum Disorder
entries.summary: Individual heterogeneity and acquisition-site variability complicate neuroimaging-based characterization of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). We propose PsyDrift, combining ASD/healthy-control-supervised functional-connectivity representations with healthy-reference latent diffusion. An encoder produces 128-dimensional representations, and a denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) learns exclusively from healthy training latents. Distance from a diffusion-denoised reconstruction provides a continuous deviation score. We evaluate 1,102 subjects from all 20 ABIDE-I sites using five-seed leave-one-site-out cross-validation. The classifier and DDPM achieve mean-site AUROCs of $0.798 \pm 0.003$ and $0.718 \pm 0.013$, respectively; uncertainties denote seed standard deviations. Matched healthy-reference scorers on the same representation achieve 0.68-0.71; the statistical significance of diffusion's modest numerical advantage remains unestablished. Within ASD, scores show weak associations with ADOS Total (Spearman $ρ= 0.108$, $p = 0.038$) and full-scale IQ ($ρ= -0.138$, $p = 0.002$), without adjustment for age, sex, site, or head motion. Frozen evaluation without retraining or hyperparameter adaptation yields pooled AUROCs of 0.69 on ABIDE-II and 0.61 on ADHD-200, providing preliminary evidence of cross-cohort and cross-disorder transfer. These results demonstrate healthy-reference deviation scoring within an ASD-supervised representation; incremental predictive and clinical value remains unestablished.
entries.comment: Extended version of a paper accepted at the CVPath-Vision4Neuro Workshop at WACV 2027. Includes expanded related-work and future-work discussion

entries.title: Learning Gaussian Process Priors with Linear Semigroups and Kinetic Regularisation
entries.summary: We introduce a semigroup-based construction of Gaussian process (GP) priors. A linear semigroup transforms a source GP at $t=0$ into a prior at $t=1$, enabling computationally tractable regression. Linearity preserves Gaussianity, allowing us to characterise the evolution of the covariance and draw connections with optimal transport and convolution models. The semigroup is parametrised by its generator, which is learned through two competing objectives: the marginal likelihood encourages agreement with observations, while a kinetic-energy regulariser favours lower-energy trajectories and limits unnecessary mass displacement from the source GP. Experiments on independent GP draws show that, with sufficiently many training functions, the learned prior provides accurate predictions on held-out functions, while kinetic regularisation substantially reduces the energy of the generated trajectories without compromising prediction accuracy.

entries.title: Constrained Diffusion from Binary Evaluations via Learned Doob h-Functions
entries.summary: Conditional generation under constraints that can only be checked on a finished sample, such as a molecular property filter, remains challenging for diffusion models: most guidance methods require differentiable measurement operators, paired conditional data, or rollouts of the base model at every step. We present a framework grounded in the Doob $h$-transform that reduces conditional generation to learning a single function, the probability that a noisy sample denoises into the constraint set. We learn this function from binary clean-sample evaluations alone, by squared-error regression on forward-noised labels; the base model is frozen, one lightweight head is trained per constraint, and noisy-state classifier guidance arises as a special case. The exact guidance step fades where the constraint signal provably vanishes and carries a factor of the inverse probability across samples, which normalized guidance discards: with the schedule and mean step size held fixed, equalizing the step costs 17.0 to 18.5 points of constraint satisfaction on CIFAR-10 at comparable FID, across independently trained estimators. Guidance is more than 50$\times$ cheaper per satisfying sample than rejection sampling at a 1.7% base rate, raises a Lipinski-type property filter on QM9 from 54.3% to 96.8%, and lifts satisfaction on Stable Diffusion 1.5 from 7.2% to 60.0% at one sixteenth of the cost of derivative-free selection, which reaches 9.0%. These results demonstrate that binary evaluations of clean samples are sufficient supervision for constrained generation across pixel, latent, and molecular diffusion.

entries.title: From Distributional to Temporal Interactions in McKean--Vlasov Games and Control
entries.summary: The paper examines the relation between time and population in stochastic games and control. The idea is to substitute the interaction described via the population law with the interaction described via the occupation measure of a single self-interacting trajectory. Thus we study how McKean--Vlasov fixed point games and Mean Field Control problems compare with their resulting self-interacting counterparts. Assuming appropriate dissipativity and regularity conditions, we find that the ergodic costs, value functions and optimal feedback sets are identical, and the fixed point equilibria are equivalent. In addition, we obtain uniform bounds on both trajectories and costs for finite horizon problems. These bounds allow proving asymptotic equivalence of the normalized value functions, and enable the transfer of equilibrium strategies and optimal feedbacks from one representation to another, with approximation errors that vanish as the horizon length increases.

entries.title: Selecting Stable Sampling Dynamics for Compositional Diffusion: A Feynman-Kac Weight Reduction
entries.summary: Given $K$ separately trained diffusion models, how should one sample from a $β_k$-weighted product of their terminal laws without jointly retraining the experts? Existing Feynman--Kac constructions provide many weighted stochastic differential equations (SDEs) with the correct target marginal. The consequential question is how to select useful proposal dynamics among them. We study an explicit family of weighted diffusions that realizes the same product-of-intermediate-experts trajectory. A scalar parameter $λ$ controls how strongly the proposal drift follows the composed expert score, while an additional Langevin component can be varied independently. Writing $B=\sum_{k=1}^{K}β_k>0$, we identify the distinguished choice $λ=1/B$. At this value, the aggregate squared-score term in the instantaneous Feynman--Kac log-weight rate cancels exactly. For positive expert exponents, the remaining score-disagreement contribution is non-positive. We call this structural cancellation Feynman--Kac reduction. Under bounded-divergence assumptions, it yields an upper bound on the instantaneous unnormalized log-weight rate for all $λ\leq 1/B$. For linear diffusion protocols with compactly supported expert data, $λ=1/B$ yields two-sided bounds at every nonterminal time, for exponents of either sign. A corresponding result holds for a single expert under the same divergence assumption. In these two-sided settings, the selected value is unique within the specified family in a universal worst-case sense. Experiments on Gaussian mixtures and molecular sampling compare the analytically predicted stability with actual sampling quality, including instances in which parameter choices different from $λ=1/B$ perform better empirically.

entries.title: Besicovitch Pseudo Almost Periodic Stochastic Processes and Their Applications to Delayed Stochastic Neural Networks
entries.summary: The Besicovitch almost periodic concept is a generalization of the Bohr, Stepanov, and Weyl almost periodic concepts and, in a certain sense, has broader coverage and weaker conditions. However, the concept of pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes in the Besicovitch sense has not yet been systematically proposed, which limits the characterization of the complex oscillatory behavior of a broader class of stochastic non-autonomous systems. This paper proposes the concept of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes. As an application of this concept, we study the existence of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic solutions in distribution for a class of stochastic delayed neural networks in which all parameters except the time delays are pseudo almost periodic and establish stability criteria for such solutions in the $p$-th mean sense. The work of this paper fills the gap caused by the lack of the concept of Besicovitch pseudo almost periodic stochastic processes and provides a new conceptual tool and analytical approach for characterizing the complex oscillatory behavior of stochastic differential equations and stochastic neural network systems.

entries.title: CrysLDM: Latent Diffusion Model for Crystal Material Generation
entries.summary: Generating new crystal materials with desirable chemical properties has long been a challenging task. Existing diffusion models operate in feature space, requiring complex diffusion architectures to model the joint distribution of atom types, coordinates, and lattice structures. This complexity increases the number of diffusion steps, leading to higher training and sampling costs. In this work, we aim to generate novel crystal materials within a time- and resource-constrained setup, where existing models are not well-suited. To address this, we propose CrysLDM, a novel latent diffusion model for 3D crystal materials, which integrates a variational autoencoder and a diffusion model. The VAE encoder maps 3D crystal structures into a latent space, where the diffusion model operates. Since CrysLDM leverages a smooth, lower-dimensional latent space, it simplifies the generative process and accelerates both training and inference. Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets and tasks, we show that CrysLDM generates stable and valid materials with quality comparable to state-of-the-art methods, while being significantly more efficient in terms of computational resources and time.

entries.title: JKO-GRPO: Augmenting GRPO with Wasserstein Proximal Steps for Flow-Matching VLAs
entries.summary: Flow-based vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_0,π_{0.5}$ generate continuous action chunks by flow matching, and online reinforcement learning (RL) can improve them beyond supervised fine-tuning. Existing methods, such as Flow-GRPO and $π_{\mathrm{RL}}$, optimize likelihood ratios of stochastic denoising transitions, which reweight the sampled actions by their advantages but do not use the distances between them. We propose JKO-GRPO, which augments Flow-GRPO with Wasserstein proximal steps, with two contributions: (1) At each state, we treat the group of sampled actions as an empirical distribution and formulate policy improvement as a Jordan-Kinderlehrer-Otto (JKO) step. We use a soft discrete $c$-transform to construct transport targets from group-relative advantages and combine shared-noise regression of the deterministic flow sampler onto these targets and combined with the clipped Flow-GRPO objective without Kullback-Leibler (KL) regularization. (2) We extend this approach to sequential VLA control through random-time branching: we select one or multiple action-chunk indices along old-policy trajectories and independently apply group-level JKO updates using candidate continuations from the corresponding states.

entries.title: Marked INAR model and the rough Hawkes--Heston limit
entries.summary: We develop a discrete-time Monte Carlo algorithm for the rough Hawkes-Heston model based on a nearly unstable marked integer-valued autoregressive (INAR) process. We implement the algorithm with a block fast Fourier transform (FFT) scheme that evaluates the excitation convolution in $O(N\log^2 N)$ operations per path on an $N$-bin grid. We prove joint convergence in law of the spot variance, log price and common marked point measure to their rough Hawkes-Heston limits. We prove convergence of European call and put option prices, as well as convergence of arithmetic Asian and down-and-out put option prices to their continuously monitored values. For European options, the one-year implied volatility smiles computed from the grid transform approach the continuous affine reference across four roughness levels. Monte Carlo experiments on the same three grids compare arithmetic Asian and down-and-out put option prices with a finer-grid reference and demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed algorithm.

entries.title: Gated Payoff-Weighted Net Profit Maximization For Online Portfolio Selection With Transaction Costs
entries.summary: In this paper, we study online portfolio selection (OLPS) problems. The net profit maximization (NPM) acting upon Adaptive Online Moving Average (AOLMA), namely the AOLNPM strategy in portfolio selection, trades when forecast gain exceeds the transaction cost. In essence, this method relies heavily on calibrated forecasts. Indeed, we show that AOLMA forecasts overstate the realized relative returns. We therefore design a gate that adjusts how strongly an AOLMA forecast is used; for each asset, it learns the recent mixture proportion assigned to AOLMA from predictive likelihoods against a neutral forecast (no change). The proportion therefore estimates the extent to which the forecast is realized. We then feed the resulting forecast into the NPM portfolio rule, where the gate acts as an asset-specific cost threshold. A payoff-weighted fund combines gated NPM experts with fixed decay factors in proportion to their wealth and needs no learning rate. On nine datasets with a transaction cost rate of 0.1%, our method produces 5.9 times the wealth of AOLNPM in geometric mean and sits above AOLNPM on every dataset, with its preponderance growing with the cost rate.

entries.title: OnCache: Learning Dynamic Caching Schedules for Efficient Diffusion Inference
entries.summary: Diffusion models have revolutionized generative tasks but incur high inference latency due to iterative denoising. Cache-based strategies accelerate inference by reusing intermediate features, yet they largely rely on static, sample-agnostic schedules. Our empirical analysis reveals two factors that these schedules overlook. (i) denoising dynamics and computational requirements vary across prompts, motivating adaptive computation allocation. (ii) sensitivity to caching errors varies across timesteps, so static schedules may reuse features at error-sensitive steps or waste computation at less sensitive ones. We therefore propose OnCache, a dynamic caching framework that makes prompt-adaptive decisions online about how much computation to allocate and when to refresh cached features. A policy is trained offline on paired compute and cache continuations from identical denoising states, using differences in terminal fidelity and the number of function evaluations (NFE) to account for the downstream consequences of each decision. To further improve the generation quality, a neural corrector compensates for caching-induced errors and mitigates their accumulation throughout the denoising trajectory. Both components are lightweight and introduce negligible additional inference latency. On FLUX.1-dev, OnCache achieves a nearly $3\times$ generation speedup at $1024^2$ resolution, with LPIPS of $0.156$ and SSIM of $0.860$. We further extend OnCache to video generation on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, achieving state-of-the-art efficiency--quality trade-offs across both modalities.

entries.title: A generalization of Lévy's stochastic area formula for Gaussian rough paths
entries.summary: In this paper, we establish a generalization of Lévy's stochastic area formula for the canonical rough path lift of a $2n$-dimensional centered Gaussian process with independent, identically distributed components. The formula extends the identity obtained by Aihara, Akahori, Fujii and Nitta [1] for Brownian motion. We compute the expectation of the exponential of a functional involving stochastic areas and quadratic forms in the terminal values. The result is expressed in terms of spectral data of a Hilbert--Schmidt operator associated with the stochastic area and an $n \times n$ determinant. We also give a necessary and sufficient condition for absolute integrability in terms of the covariance at the terminal time and the symmetric part of the quadratic form in the terminal values. As examples, we discuss the cases of fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $1/4<H<1$, Brownian motion and the Brownian bridge. In particular, we recover the formula in [1] under the exact condition for absolute integrability.

entries.title: Reward Tilting via Semantic Noising
entries.summary: Steering a generative model toward a desired property typically requires separate fine-tuning for each reward or additional computation during sampling. We propose semantic noising, which conditions generation on a noisy semantic representation of the data. The resulting posteriors correspond to exponential tilts by linear-quadratic rewards in semantic space, allowing a single model to support objectives and strengths chosen after training. A conditional generator can be trained to approximate these posteriors directly, while models that generate semantic representations by diffusion provide analytic tilted denoisers for the same family of rewards. We illustrate semantic noising in three settings. An autoregressive molecular generator trained with semantic noising controls properties individually and jointly, with a better reward--KL trade-off than property-conditioned models. On ImageNet, a joint diffusion model of images and their CLIP embeddings achieves FID comparable to REG, and tilting it toward a higher aesthetic score matches the best of 16 samples at the cost of a single sample. Finally, pretrained factorized models such as Kandinsky 2.2 support the same tilts without retraining.

entries.title: Systems of quadratic BSDEs with unbounded terminal data
entries.summary: The paper is devoted to global solution of multidimensional backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) with non-convex quadratic generators and unbounded terminal data. The generators of some individual BSDEs of the system are allowed to have interactions among their second unknown variables and can be non-Lipschitz continuous with general growth in the first unknown variable $y$ and non-convex/non-concave in the second unknown variable $z$. We extend the results of the authors' previous paper [JDE, 2023] by incorporating both the no convexity/concavity of the generators and the interaction among the second unknown variables of individual BSDEs, and update the assumptions of Theorems 2.10 and 2.27 stated in the authors' previous paper~[EJP, 2025] so as to fill in a gap in the original proofs.

entries.title: The broken-sample problem revisited II: Detecting hidden linear dependencies
entries.summary: We study the detection problem for shuffled linear regression, in which the covariates and the responses are either independent or linearly related through a latent correspondence. Consider independent standard Gaussian covariates \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\in\mathbb R^d\) and scalar responses \(Y_1,\ldots,Y_n\). In a shuffled linear model, \(Y_i=\langle X_{π_*(i)},β_*\rangle+σZ_i\), where both the permutation \(π_*\) and the regression coefficient $β_*$ are latent and $Z_i$'s are white Gaussian noise. The goal is to distinguish this model from one in which the covariates and responses are independent with the same marginal distribution. In the low-dimensional regime of $d \ll \frac{\log n}{\log\log n}$, we show that the detection threshold is given by $σ=o(1)$ for fixed $d$ and $σ^2 = Θ(\frac{1}{d\log d})$ for growing $d$; both thresholds are achieved in nearly linear time using moment-based test statistics inspired by matched filters in signal processing. For higher dimensions, tests based on sliced Wasserstein distance succeed when $σ^2 = o(\frac{1}{(d\log d)^2})$, while the optimal threshold remains open. As a by-product, we show that the shuffled linear model exhibits an ``all-or-nothing'' phase transition for estimating $β_*$ at $σ^2\asymp \frac{1}{d\log d}$ in low dimensions. In particular, $β_*$ can be consistently estimated in nearly linear time, even when it is information-theoretically impossible to recover any positive fraction of the latent matching $π^*$.

entries.title: The dimension of optimal plans in multi-marginal optimal transport
entries.summary: For general cost functions, we determine the maximal dimension on which solutions to the multi-marginal optimal transport problem with absolutely continuous marginals are concentrated. The dimension is obtained via a novel characteristic integer associated with the Hessian of the cost function. Applications are given to important examples of multi-marginal problems like Wasserstein barycenters, Wasserstein cubic splines and Brenier's generalized Euler equations.

entries.title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
entries.summary: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

entries.title: RadAG: Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance for Efficient Inference-Time Alignment of Diffusion Models
entries.summary: Diffusion and flow-based models have achieved remarkable success in generation, yet their samples often remain suboptimal in fidelity and text alignment. Two lines of inference-time methods address this: extrapolation guidance, such as classifier-free guidance (CFG) and its variants, and reward guidance, which aligns samples with reward models of human preference. Extrapolation guidance needs only forward passes, but it builds its reference by heuristic rules unrelated to the reward and therefore cannot steer sampling toward a given reward. Gradient-based reward guidance steers sampling directly toward a higher reward, but backpropagates through the entire generator at every step. This trade-off raises the question of whether extrapolation guidance can steer sampling toward a higher reward without a full backward pass. To answer this, we introduce Reward-Adversarial Attention Guidance (RadAG), which constructs the reference by perturbing the attention logits of a single block against their reward gradient and extrapolates away from it. We prove that this update increases the reward of the clean estimate to first order, while its backward pass stops at the perturbed block instead of traversing the entire generator. On FLUX.2-klein-4B and 9B with PickScore and aesthetic rewards, RadAG achieves the highest target reward in every setting with 30-65% less time than gradient-based and candidate-based baselines.

entries.title: Contrastive Gradient Guidance for Test-Time Multi-Preference Alignment of Diffusion Models
entries.summary: Aligning pre-trained diffusion models with multiple context-dependent preferences requires adapting generation at test time rather than relying on offline fine-tuning, which requires hyperparameter tuning and a new training run for each preference trade-off. Existing approaches compress diverse preferences into a single scalar reward objective for fine-tuning or test-time guidance rather than directly reusing existing generative experts released for different purposes and obtained through different fine-tuning methods. In this work, we propose Contrastive Gradient Guidance (CGG), a test-time compositional generative framework that reformulates multi-preference alignment as a composition of distributions. CGG represents each preference as a contrastive preference pair of favored experts and unfavored anti-experts, whose score difference forms a contrastive gradient guidance signal that combines denoising directions (gradients) from off-the-shelf diffusion models during sampling. Experiments show that CGG reuses pre-trained and fine-tuned models as favored experts or anti-experts to control output style and safety, and that it can be combined with existing sampling-based reward guidance. With a single fixed scale per pair, CGG composes five preferences at once and gives a more balanced trade-off across text-image preference, concept control, photographic fidelity, and safety than offline fine-tuning, weight-space merging, and reward steering.

entries.title: Wavelet-CFM for the extragalactic millimeter-wave sky
entries.summary: We develop a Wavelet-factorized Conditional Flow Matching (Wavelet-CFM) framework to generate fast, accurate simulations of correlated astrophysical fields including gravitational lensing convergence ($κ$), the kinetic and thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich (kSZ and tSZ) effects, and cosmic infrared background (CIB) emission. Together these make up every bright extragalactic component of the millimeter-wave (mm-wave) sky apart from radio sources. Our approach combines multi-scale wavelet decomposition with conditional flow matching models, trained on $\sim$9$\times$9 deg$^2$ patches at 1-arcminute resolution. The four fields are generated jointly, including their cross couplings, and the model has a tractable likelihood, which to our knowledge has not previously been achieved for this set of components. The power spectra, one-point distributions and Minkowski functionals of the generated maps match a validation set to a few percent. These results show promise for enabling field-level cosmological analyses of mm-wave data.
entries.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Accepted to the 9th Machine Learning and the Physical Sciences Workshop (ML4PS)

entries.title: Neural Schrödinger Bridge via Yasue Action with Applications to Generative Modeling
entries.summary: We propose a novel neural solver for inferring the continuous state evolution of the Schrödinger bridge problem. The proposed solver builds on a saddle point formulation involving the Yasue action functional. This allows us to realize the continuous state evolution by learning the optimal velocity for an ordinary differential equation, as opposed to learning the optimal drift for a stochastic differential equation. The proposed solver only uses the source and the target samples, and not the source and target distributions per se, which makes it particularly suitable for high dimensional applications arising in generative modeling. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed solver using several numerical experiments in low and high dimensions, using both real and synthetic datasets.

entries.title: Interpreting Diffusion Model Activations in Natural Language
entries.summary: Interpreting the intermediate activations of diffusion models (DMs) is key to understanding how they generate images. Existing interpretability methods for DMs provide limited support for open-ended interrogation, making it difficult to extract human-interpretable insights. We extend LatentQA, the task of answering natural-language questions about Large Language Model activations, to DM activations. We introduce the Diffusion-specific Activation Oracle (DAO), which translates DM activations into natural-language answers to open-ended questions about the ongoing generation. Our experiments show that DAO can effectively describe the content of the final image from activations at early denoising steps. Additionally, we demonstrate that DAO captures the structure of the DM's activation space well enough to steer image generation toward target attributes. Furthermore, we show that attribution patching through DAO identifies DM components that contribute to visual attributes specified in natural language. Our code is available at https://github.com/yamanoko/dao/tree/main.

entries.title: Limit distributions and bootstrap for smooth adapted Wasserstein distances
entries.summary: In this paper, we provide limit theorems for the Gaussian-smoothed adapted Wasserstein distances. Let $\widehatμ_n$ be the empirical measure of independent paths with law $μ$ on $(\mathbb{R}^d)^T$. Let $P = μ* γ_σ$ and $P_n = \widehatμ_n * γ_σ$, where $γ_σ= N(0,σ^2 I_{dT})$ is a Gaussian measure with mean zero and covariance matrix $σ^2 I_{dT}$. We first assume that $μ$ is compactly supported. For every $1 < p < \infty$ and fixed $d, T$, and $σ> 0$, we show that $\sqrt{n}\,\mathrm{AW}_p(P_n,P) \Rightarrow Q_{P,p}(G)^{1/p}$, where $G$ is the Gaussian limit of the density fluctuation and $Q_{P,p}$ is the minimum adapted $p$-energy for the linearized continuity equation. We prove full-path bootstrap consistency and the convergence of the first and $p$-th moments. The limit and the bootstrap hold for noncompact laws as well, for all $1 < p < \infty$ under appropriate tail and structural conditions. For two-sided bounded density perturbations of strongly log-concave laws, the bandwidth is not restricted for $1 < p \le 2$. For $p > 2$, we give sufficient tail conditions and provide a Gaussian counterexample where root-$n$ tightness fails for small bandwidths. Our proof is based on a two-endpoint local expansion of bicausal transport. As an application, we provide asymptotic error bounds for optimal stopping values under the smoothed model using the bootstrap quantiles.

entries.title: Guidance-Induced Activation of Score Estimation Errors in Diffusion Models
entries.summary: Classifier-free guidance (CFG) combines conditional and unconditional score estimates to steer diffusion sampling. The weighted-solenoidal component of each score error has no instantaneous effect on the evolution of its corresponding reference density. Because the guided density in CFG generally differs from both reference densities, the combination of these solenoidal components can affect the evolution of the guided marginals. We call this mechanism guidance-induced error activation. Using a weighted Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition, we identify the activated error field, quantify its magnitude, and characterize when it vanishes. At fixed noise time, the activated error field varies continuously with guidance strength. Its weak first-order variation has two terms, one from reweighting the errors and one from the change in the guided density. For finite score errors, ODE characteristics and an SDE Feynman-Kac formula connect error-activation to the generated densities. For a class of finite Gaussian mixtures, error-activation can account for most of the KL divergence between the generated distributions by learned-score and exact-score CFG ODE samplers under strong guidance. Ideal score filtering removes the weighted-solenoidal errors and eliminates error-activation. Controlled experiments with Gaussian and Gamma mixtures illustrate how activation affects the generated densities. Qualitative CIFAR-10 comparisons suggest that filtering can help preserve object structure under strong guidance.

entries.title: Which Loans, Not How Many: Exactly Level-Invariant, Anytime-Valid Monitoring of Deployed Risk Models
entries.summary: A refinancing wave can change the number of mortgage prepayments without changing the relationship between scores and prepayment. In a logistic model, conditioning on the monthly count removes the intercept from the likelihood of which loans prepay. Our fixed-start slope product tests a lower bound on the calibration slope. At threshold 20 its probability of ever crossing under the null is at most 5%. The restarted level sum tracks departures from intercept tolerance. A confidence sequence estimates a constant slope, and the restart-intersection rule detects changes in that slope. A continuous mixture avoids the off-grid width floor of a discrete prior. On Freddie Mac loans, fixed-slope resampling reproduces 78% of maintained-model monthly AUC variance in development and 70% in the holdout (95% intervals 57-100% and 48-100%). From fresh holdout starts, the restarted level sum crosses on both paths, and the fixed-start slope product stays below threshold on both. The restart-intersection rule signals a downward change for the frozen model in April 2018 and an upward change for the maintained model in a supplementary run in August 2019.

entries.title: Neural Fidelity Calibration for Informative Sim-to-Real Adaptation
entries.summary: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) can transfer agile robot skills from simulation to the real world, but closing the sim-to-real gap by domain randomization requires expert physics knowledge, and simulator calibration from real data typically targets a few hand-picked parameters. Even then, simulators miss real-world effects, and environments reconstructed from onboard perception inherit sensing errors that limit policy improvement. We propose Neural Fidelity Calibration (NFC), which uses conditional flow matching to calibrate simulator physical parameters and residual fidelity domains online during deployment. Residual fidelity captures sim-to-real dynamics discrepancies and perception-induced environment uncertainty. NFC operates in a latent space so that realistic environments can be sampled from the inferred posterior for real-to-sim policy fine-tuning. The framework is informative: the pretrained policy is fine-tuned only when an anomaly is detected, sequential NFC seeds its proposal from the simulation-pretrained estimator, and a hallucination policy modulates posterior uncertainty following optimism in the face of uncertainty. NFC attains the most accurate posteriors among established simulation-based inference methods on five robots with up to 39 physical parameters and a 128x128 residual terrain. On a wheeled robot with a broken wheel axle deployed on snow, mud, and wet grass, NFC raises success on rough terrain from 26% to 70% and reduces orientation jerk by 88%. Code and videos will be released upon publication.
entries.comment: The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/nfc/

entries.title: Epidemic random model under vaccination regime and non-permanent immunity driven by time-changed Levy noise
entries.summary: A random version of the Susceptible-Infected-Recovered-Vaccinated (SIRV) epidemic model with non-permanent immunity and a population of non-constant size is studied. The compartments satisfy a system of differential equations in which the contact rate is a random coefficient, and the contact rate itself is driven by a stochastic differential equation with time-changed Levy noise. This noise is constructed from a conditional Brownian motion and a doubly stochastic Poisson random field, both governed by a stochastic clock. When the clock is independent of the Brownian and Poisson components, the two parts of the noise are a time-changed Brownian motion and a time-changed Poisson random measure. The equation for the contact rate decouples from the compartment equations and enters them as a random parameter, which allows the compartments to be treated pathwise. The existence, uniqueness, and positivity of the global solution are proven, and the basic reproduction number of the model is shown to be random. Furthermore, sufficient conditions for extinction and persistence in mean of the disease are derived. The conditions are expressed in terms of the parameters of the model and two long-run characteristics.

entries.title: Learning the Projection onto the Data Support: Distribution Learning that Avoids Memorization
entries.summary: We introduce a framework for learning distributions supported on manifolds based on estimating the nearest-point projection onto the data support. Specifically, we define an objective functional over a class of functions whose minimizer recovers this projection. The proposed framework automatically adapts to the intrinsic dimension and allows for data supported on unions of manifolds with varying dimensions. The resulting objective can be optimized using standard neural network architectures. We present population-level results establishing recovery of the manifold projection and prove finite-sample Wasserstein generalization bounds. Furthermore, we validate the approach empirically across a range of settings. In contrast to widely used generative models such as diffusion models, whose objectives can be minimized by memorizing training samples, our formulation excludes such behavior. We also introduce a direct memorization metric to verify that the learned projection generates new samples rather than reproducing the training set.

entries.title: Topology Hub Optimal Transport: Eliminating Long Context Dilution at Flash Speed
entries.summary: Long-context models use sparse or structured attention to avoid quadratic cost, yet retrieving a small set of relevant facts embedded among hundreds of thousands of distractors degrades as normalization mass disperses with length. Hub-and-spoke optimal transport (OT) replaces the dense $L \times L$ matrix with a linear-size graph over local windows and $K$ shared hubs balanced by Sinkhorn scaling. Building on block-wise tail refinement and fixed-support transport topology (arXiv:2605.08123, arXiv:2609.07954), we introduce Topology Hub Optimal Transport (THOT): (1) bounded-support capacity gating via simplex sparsemax ($O(L\log L)$) or sorting-free token-local thresholded ReLU ($O(L)$), driving excess distractor mass to zero; (2) a three-sweep $1+2$ annealed row-closed Sinkhorn schedule that damps bipartite residuals; (3) an exact rank-$(D+2R+1)$ One-Reference-Tile adjoint in batched split-factor Triton kernels (BF16 Tensor Cores, FP32 potentials); and (4) a chunked exclusive-prefix causal variant with verified zero future leakage. On NVIDIA L4, sparsemax THOT trained at $L=128$ reaches 97.40% zero-shot recall of fixed bindings at $L=262{,}144$ under pure task loss ($α=0$) and 98.83% at $α=0.05$ (matched by $O(L)$ thresholded ReLU at $α=0.05$, vs. 80.60% at $α=0$), while softmax-gated hub OT drops to 3.52%. In bidirectional operator microbenchmarks, our kernel runs forward+VJP in 100.1 ms at $H=8, D=64, L=262\mathrm{K}$ (2.2x faster with 4.0x smaller compiler temporaries than latent softmax) and 1.34 ms vs. 4.37 ms for cuDNN FlashAttention at $L=4{,}096$; multi-layer LM runs use the unfused path. Zero-shot WikiText-103 multi-needle retrieval hits 100.00% (128/128 queries at $L=65\mathrm{K}$) vs. 0.78% for short-trained RoPE FlashAttention, and compact 4-layer WikiText-4K runs show modest causal and masked LM gains.

entries.title: From Gist to Verbatim: The Controllable Path of One Image Through a Diffusion Prior
entries.summary: Modern generative models are typically studied for their ability to generalize, while memorization is treated as a failure mode. We invert this perspective and ask how a generative model can recall a single datum. We frame memorization as a control problem: a learned conditioning signal steers a frozen diffusion model toward a target image, and we follow the formation of this memory throughout training. Before converging to exact reproduction (verbatim), memory passes through a regime of abstraction: samples preserve the target's semantic content (gist) while remaining diverse in appearance, leaving predictable detail to the generative prior. This semantic organization emerges despite the absence of labels, captions, or any explicit semantic objective. In the abstraction regime, the learned memory approaches ordinary text conditioning and supports editing, one-shot recognition, and retrieval more effectively than in the near-perfect reconstruction regime. These results suggest that memorization can serve as a probe of the relevance structure encoded by a generative model: what must be stored about a datum, what can be reconstructed from prior knowledge, and how learned memories interpolate between reconstructive recall and literal data storage.

entries.title: Beyond Visual Fidelity: Comparing Categorical and Continuous World Models
entries.summary: Visual world models can now generate compelling interactive worlds, but visual realism does not guarantee faithful dynamics. We systematically compare how categorical and continuous prediction shape learned dynamics under both next-token and iterative whole-frame generation. These choices are often bundled in approaches such as autoregressive token models and whole-frame flow matching. We design controlled 2D and 3D environments and evaluate dynamics validity, calibration, and visual quality. In 2D with lossless visual encoding, categorical models achieve higher rollout validity with less training compute, particularly for stochastic entities. Among categorical models, greedy decoding produces the highest rollout validity, while sampling from a next-token model yields the best-calibrated stochastic predictions. Failures in continuous models, such as disappearing game characters, echo those seen in more complex environments. Here, known dynamics let us measure their impact. In 3D, categorical models also achieve stronger long-horizon performance with less training compute. Even models with lossy tokenization remain competitive on semantic accuracy and FVD, despite lower next-frame RGB accuracy. Together, these findings make a strong case for categorical prediction as a compute-efficient route to learning world dynamics.

entries.title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers
entries.summary: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.

entries.title: Graph Signal Generation via Graph-Aware Diffusion Models
entries.summary: Many signals are defined on the nodes of a graph, such as traffic flow at road sensors or user purchases of related products. They are often partly observed, and learning their distribution enables imputing missing values and forecasting future ones. Diffusion models learn such distributions, but their forward noise is independent across nodes and does not depend on the graph. We introduce graph-aware diffusion (GAD), whose forward process is a heat diffusion on the graph driven by Gaussian noise. In the graph Fourier basis, the forward transition is a scalar Gaussian channel at each frequency. With a shared diffusion rate, high graph frequencies are attenuated faster than low ones. We propose Mode-Adaptive SNR Scheduling (MASS), which assigns each graph frequency its own diffusion rate and keeps all of them at the same SNR. For graph-stationary signals, MASS equalizes the normalized error of the optimal linear denoiser across frequencies. We bound reverse-SDE stiffness as a function of the (shifted) Laplacian's condition number, with a logarithmic upper bound for MASS and a linear lower bound for shared rates. GAD with MASS improves recommendation accuracy by 5-19%, reduces traffic-imputation RMSE by up to 7.8% with half as many reverse steps, and improves forecasting MAE and RMSE using only 3 reverse steps.
entries.comment: 19 pages, 2 figures, 9 tables. Under review at IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence. Code: https://github.com/vimalkb7/SpectralAnalysisGAD

entries.title: Sampling non-abelian lattice gauge theories with diffusion models
entries.summary: We present gauge-equivariant diffusion models as samplers for lattice gauge theories (LGTs). Using lattice gauge-equivariant convolutional neural networks (L-CNNs) and the Metropolis-adjusted annealed Langevin algorithm (MAALA), we are able to accurately sample two-dimensional U(2) field configurations and show first promising results for four-dimensional SU(3). Our two-dimensional models extrapolate remarkably well to larger inverse couplings than originally trained on. We confirm this by comparing observables to analytically known values and to hybrid Monte Carlo results.
entries.comment: 7 pages, 4 figures, contribution to the Proceedings of the 22nd International Conference on QCD in Extreme Conditions (xQCD 2026), 14-17 July 2026, Busan, Korea

entries.title: $L^1$ stability of the entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$ without moment assumptions
entries.summary: We establish qualitative stability in $L^1$ and Ruzsa distance for Shannon's entropy power inequality in $\mathbb{R}^d$, without any moment assumptions. The proof uses the optimal transport argument by Rioul (2017), majorization bounds of density rearrangements, and the stability of the sharp form of Young's inequality due to Christ (2019). Along the way we also extend recent one-dimensional results on de Bruijn's identity, the continuity of differential entropy, and the equality case of the entropy power inequality to random vectors of any dimension.

entries.title: Small noise limit for Entropic Variational Mean-Field Games
entries.summary: We study second order variational mean-field games with quadratic Hamiltonian. In analogy with entropic optimal transport, Benamou, Carlier, Di Marino and the second author recently proposed an entropy-minimization formulation of the problem, which could be interpreted as the Lagrangian counterpart of the classical Eulerian approach. We investigate the small-noise $Γ$-limit for the Lagrangian entropy-minimization formulation and establish $Γ$-convergence of second order mean-field games towards their deterministic first order counterpart. This also translates into another (dynamical) proof of the convergence of the Schrödinger problem to optimal transport. Moreover, we study the original Eulerian problem and prove a first order energy expansion, which establishes a selection principle for minimizers of the deterministic problem.

entries.title: Late-Time Dynamics of Flow Matching: Distance Geometry and Learning
entries.summary: Generative models transform simple random inputs into samples that resemble observed data. For a finite training set, a central question is how its geometry shapes the terminal dynamics and the probabilities assigned to individual samples. We address this question for flow matching with linear interpolation between independent Gaussian and empirical samples. The squared distance to the training set generates explicit paths contracting exponentially toward the nearest sample. We prove that exact trajectories restarted at prescribed late-time states approximate these paths uniformly over all elapsed times and compact sets of starting states away from Voronoi interfaces, with an error exponentially small in the inverse squared restart noise scale. The initial mass near interfaces controls the quadratic Wasserstein error between the exact and reference laws. For Gaussian and fixed Gaussian-tube restart laws, this gives a square-root rate in the restart noise scale, uniform over time, which a two-site example shows to be sharp in general. At ties, the Clarke subdifferential characterizes the graphical limit of the rescaled velocity field. This geometry motivates two learning methods: fitting the distance potential with value and gradient supervision, and fitting velocities along explicit contraction paths. A transport estimate separates initialization mismatch, velocity error, incomplete contraction, and endpoint allocation. MNIST experiments illustrate the distinct roles of support proximity, nearest-site retention, and feature fidelity. These results connect flow matching and score-based diffusion through a common limiting geometry and show how asymptotic analysis can inform the design and evaluation of generative models.

entries.title: Beyond Resolution: Inference-Time Parameterized Temporal Consistency in Generative Regional Climate Downscaling
entries.summary: GCM-to-RCM downscaling emulation is dominated by generative diffusion models, but most existing work evaluates skill only per timestep, treating each field as an independent snapshot. This leaves open whether generated sequences are temporally coherent or merely independently plausible, a gap that matters increasingly for sub-daily resolutions since downstream impacts depend on accumulation and persistence, not just on isolated states. This study asks whether autoregressive conditioning can deliver coherent rollouts without error accumulation and ensemble-spread collapse, and whether a single model can expose the resulting coherence-diversity trade-off as a controllable inference choice rather than a fixed design commitment. We introduce a noise-conditioned teacher-forcing training scheme conditioning a diffusion U-Net downscaling model on a noised previous high-resolution state, so the trained model interpolates continuously between autoregressive (AR) and per-timestep independent (PTI) sampling via one noise parameter. We apply the scheme to an hourly, European-domain historical simulation downscaling AWI-CM1 (1$^\circ$) with ICON (0.11$^\circ$, regridded to 0.25$^\circ$) for precipitation and 2-meter temperature. The noise parameter traces a smooth interpolation between ICON's autocorrelation and PTI generation. AR rollouts of up to six months show no progressive degradation, with ensemble spread contracting only slightly within the first 24 hours. In contrast, the same architecture trained on noise-free previous states diverges. For precipitation PTI underestimates maxima by up to 2x in daily aggregations, while AR tracks ICON's maxima closely. For temperature, differences between modes are negligible. These results show that in diffusion downscaling temporal consistency can be achieved architecture-agnostically and offered as a controllable, not fixed, inference choice.

entries.title: Stochastic Differential Equations on the Simplex
entries.summary: We propose a framework for simplex-valued diffusion processes, formulated as solutions to stochastic differential equations driven by antisymmetric Brownian motion. Our edge-wise representation includes the multivariate Jacobi processes and the general class of continuous simplex-valued polynomial diffusions. Also, it allows bounded, locally Lipschitz state-dependent drift rates and edge weights. We establish weak solutions, as well as global strong existence and pathwise uniqueness for strictly positive initial states under a sufficient boundary non-attainment condition.

entries.title: Preserving Pretrained CFG Structure in RL for Diffusion Models with Conditional Contrast Regularization
entries.summary: Reinforcement Learning (RL) has become an important component in the post-training of diffusion models. In practice, however, standard RL often improves the target reward without reliably preserving holistic generation quality, leading to unstable reward-quality trade-offs that we view as a form of reward hacking. Since Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) is known to improve visual clarity, prompt alignment, and perceptual quality in generation, we investigate whether its underlying structure can serve as a useful prior during RL. We present a unified geometric view that interprets both CFG and RL as correction vectors in a common prediction space, and identify the projection of the RL-induced correction onto the pretrained CFG correction as a useful diagnostic of quality-related structural preservation. Geometric analysis and rotation intervention further show that the pretrained CFG direction carries information useful for generation quality that reward-driven RL updates do not necessarily preserve. Based on this insight, we propose Conditional Contrast Regularization (CCR), which uses the frozen reference model's conditional contrast as a local structural prior during RL. Experiments across multiple reward settings and backbones show that CCR more consistently preserves generation quality while maintaining competitive reward, yielding a better reward-quality trade-off than standard RL and generic regularization methods.

entries.title: Semiparametric Efficiency for Entropic Optimal Transport under Structured Distribution Shift
entries.summary: Can structural information improve estimation of entropic optimal transport (EOT), and when is the gain zero? We study a fixed-dimensional exponential density ratio model (DRM) with a nonparametric baseline, compact support, and fixed positive regularization. At positive limiting sampling fractions, an exact projection identity quantifies the variance gain from the restriction. The pooled empirical-likelihood estimator attains the restricted bound and supports asymptotically valid confidence intervals when the bound is positive. Even under correct specification, the gain can be zero and can shrink as the tilt space expands. The same projection residual determines direction-specific first-order bias under local misspecification. When both samples grow and the target fraction vanishes, a zero first-order tilt derivative can leave source fluctuations and quadratic tilt error as the leading terms. Their balance gives a phase transition in the limiting distribution. A continuous example gives different convergence rates for two correctly specified bases at the same distribution pair. Controlled experiments assess the fixed-proportion theory. Natural-data comparisons distinguish variance reductions from improvements in reference RMSE driven by smaller reference bias.

entries.title: Hierarchical Hybrid-Coordinate Flow Matching for Accurate and Physically Plausible Apo-to-Holo Protein Generation
entries.summary: Predicting holo-like protein conformations from apo structures is essential in structure-based drug design. Most existing apo-to-holo models operate in Cartesian space and achieve strong global accuracy. However, high global accuracy does not ensure physically valid local backbone geometry. Internal-coordinate models offer local control and validity, but regressive generation can amplify angular errors, known as the lever-arm effect. We introduce CrypticFlow, a hierarchical flow-matching model that combines these two complementary representations. An ESM-3-conditioned E(3)-equivariant graph network first generates sparse C$α$ anchors in Cartesian space. A conditional midpoint Transformer then recursively fills the gaps in local internal coordinates. During recursive generation, the decoder constrains the distance between each midpoint and any sequence-adjacent parent anchor to the corresponding apo C$α$-C$α$ distance. On the D3PM test split, CrypticFlow achieves the lowest median and mean C$α$ RMSD at published baseline capacities. Across five independent training models, the median and mean direct RMSD are 1.333 $\pm$ 0.056 angstroms and 2.766 $\pm$ 0.041 angstroms, respectively. The quality of local geometry also improves substantially. Our model achieves 99.58 $\pm$ 0.02% adjacent-distance fidelity and 95.87 $\pm$ 0.25% pseudo-angle fidelity, measured within 0.2 angstroms and 20° of the holo reference. Then, we reconstruct the predicted C$α$-only traces into all-atom structures using the cg2all coarse-to-all-atom backmapping method and evaluate their physical and geometric quality with MolProbity. Our model achieves a MolProbity score of 3.034 $\pm$ 0.054, outperforming the evaluated baselines. These results show that a hierarchical flow-matching model with hybrid coordinates can recover global accuracy while retaining local fidelity.

entries.title: Distributional Algebro-Geometric Persistence (dAGP): Wasserstein-Stable Polynomial-Relation Signatures
entries.summary: A circle and a quartic superellipse have the same homology, but their defining equations have degrees two and four, respectively. We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $μ$ on $Ω=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $φ_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(μ)=\mathbb{E}_{X\simμ}[φ_m(X)φ_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(μ)c=\mathbb{E}_μ[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $μ$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $μ\mapsto G_m(μ)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range. A $100$-repetition sensitivity study quantifies onset recovery and shows that the count grid and two continuous spectral baselines nearly saturate the four-family discrimination task.
entries.comment: 16 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Geometric Distributional Deep Learning (GDDL)

entries.title: Semigroup Hessian Estimates for Underdamped Langevin Dynamics
entries.summary:
For the semigroup $e^{t\mathcal L}$ of the underdamped Langevin dynamics, we bound the Hessian $
abla^2(e^{t\mathcal L}f)$ when $
abla f$ is uniformly bounded. When the potential is strongly convex outside a ball and has bounded second and third derivatives, and the damping rate is above an explicit threshold, the bounds on $
abla^2(e^{t\mathcal L}f)$ decay exponentially in time with constants free of the dimension. The proof combines the Wasserstein contraction of the dynamics with a Bismut--Elworthy--Li formula for the degenerate noise. As an application, we prove the uniform-in-time error of the stochastic gradient UBU integrator, with an explicit coefficient of the numerical bias in the step size, proportional to the covariance of the stochastic gradient noise.

entries.title: Memorization and Generalization in Generative Models: A Perspective From Energy-based Modeling and Associative Memory
entries.summary: Generative models now write working code, produce realistic images, and hold long conversations, yet the mechanisms behind their intelligence still evade our understanding. This thesis explores that puzzle through Associative Memory (AM), in which patterns are stored as energy minima and retrieved through attractor dynamics. Beyond their capacity, AMs form new minima known as spurious states, long regarded as a failure of memory. We argue that this failure is where creativity begins, and that memorization and generalization can coexist as outcomes of one retrieval process. First, we show that diffusion models behave as AMs. With little data, a diffusion model forms a distinct basin of attraction around each training sample. As the data grows, these basins shrink, and spurious states emerge as attractors that blend stored samples yet match none of them. They are the first signs of generative capability. We characterize this transition by measuring the volume, energy, and curvature of these basins across datasets and architectures, including Stable Diffusion. We then turn to language and move beyond the energy-based view of AM. We show that uniform-state discrete diffusion models are AMs capable of retrieving unseen data, with basins of attraction that arise from conditional likelihood maximization alone. As the training set grows, basins around training examples contract while basins around unseen examples expand, until corrupted test sentences are recovered as reliably as training ones. Conditional entropy exposes this coexistence within a single sequence and cheaply diagnoses where a model lies along the transition. Together, these results suggest that AM is a general principle defined by basins of attraction, and that memorization and generalization can coexist within one model. AM thus offers a framework for asking when a generative model recalls and when it creates.
entries.comment: A thesis that discusses the coexistence of memorization and generalization in generative models

entries.title: Are Calibrated Decision Models Calibrated on Markets? Geolocated News, Markov Switching and a System One Model for Nasdaq-100 Allocation
entries.summary: Portfolio allocation is driven by probabilities of losses, not only by forecasts of the direction (up/down) of the market. A decision model such as Jev returns a probability for a yes/no question and has been reported to be well calibrated on a set of benchmarks. However, the model's calibration against realised market outcomes has not been tested. In this study, every Friday we ask whether the Nasdaq-100 will close lower four weeks later and compare a two-regime Markov-switching model estimated on data from 1990 to 2026, Jev reading weekly headlines and geolocated news features computed with spatial queries in PostGIS, and their combination. A knowledge probe shows that Jev knows events up to late 2024, so we evaluate it on 88 weeks from January 2025 onwards. None of the models predicts the direction better than the historical base rate. A key finding is that raw Jev overestimates the probability of a decline: its mean forecast is 0.48 against an observed frequency of 0.38, and its ECE is 0.10. A prior shift to the historical base rate, which uses no outcomes from the test period, lowers the ECE to 0.015. In contrast, Platt scaling, isotonic regression and the combination with the Markov model all make the forecasts worse. In a half-Kelly allocation, the raw Jev strategy returns 3.1% per year, whereas after the prior shift it returns 14.5%; a simple buy-and-hold strategy in QQQ returns 15.3% per year. The Markov model forecasts large declines (more than 10%) well, with an AUC of 0.81, and its strategy has the highest Sharpe ratio over 1999-2026. Asked about such a large decline (base rate 4%), raw Jev forecasts 16-24% on average, and the same prior shift removes this offset. The practical lesson is that decision-model probabilities must be anchored to the base rate of the market event before they are used to size positions.

entries.title: Path-Independent Deleveraging Rules
entries.summary: We characterise path-independent auto-deleveraging (ADL) rules as an extended log-exponential family. Immunity to account splitting, merging and reopening further restrict the class. Homogeneity (essentially) restricts the class to a one-parameter family ordered by both fairness and platform risk. Its split-proof members continuously interpolate between proportional division and water-filling. Among these rules, decreasing the parameter reduces risk at the cost of increasing inequality in how accounts are treated. This suggests selecting the parameter through an ex-ante calibration to a risk bound on historical data to choose a maximally fair rule subject to that bound. A counterfactual replay of Hyperliquid's ADL episode on 10 October 2025 finds that a range of intermediate parameters significantly improves on the observed allocation in both burden dispersion and subsequent risk statistics.

entries.title: The Rate of Convergence of Empirical $(p,q)$-Gromov-Wasserstein Distances
entries.summary: We study empirical convergence rates for $(p,q)$-Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) distances $D_{p,q}$ for arbitrary real exponents $p>0$ and $q\ge1$. Let $μ$ and $ν$ be probability measures on compact metric spaces $\mathcal{X}$ and $\mathcal{Y}$, and let $\widehatμ_n$ and $\widehatν_m$ be their empirical measures, constructed from independent i.i.d. samples of sizes $n$ and $m$. If the spaces $\mathcal{X},\,\mathcal{Y}$ are compact subsets of the Euclidean spaces $\mathbb{R}^{d_x}$ and $\mathbb{R}^{d_y}$, respectively, we obtain an upper bound of order $(n\wedge m)^{-(p\wedge2)/((d_x\wedge d_y)\vee 2(p\wedge2))}$ on the plug-in error of $D_{p,q}^p(\widehatμ_n,\widehatν_m)$ in expectation, up to a logarithmic factor at the critical dimension $d_x\wedge d_y=2(p\wedge2)$. On Euclidean balls, this rate is sharp up to the logarithmic factor. More generally, we show that the same upper bound holds when one space is a compact subset of a complete, connected $d$-dimensional Riemannian manifold and the other has polynomial covering numbers, with $d_x\wedge d_y$ replaced by $d$. Earlier works on $(2,2)$-GW, $(2,1)$-GW and other even-order cases rely on variational representations of GW distances that are specific to their exponents. We instead reduce the plug-in error to an analysis of empirical processes through local duality, which may be of independent interest.
